Outcome_variable.evidence_source: [/page/13/Text/2] Table 5 shows the first model of the slope of life satisfaction. The slope of life satisfaction of the oldest old group was significantly associated with time, self-reported health, poverty level, family relationship satisfaction, and self-esteem. [...] The results revealed that trajectories of life satisfaction increased with time, good family relationships, and higher perceived health. [/page/13/Text/3] Further, in Level 2, self-esteem only had a significant effect on the slope of life satisfaction (b=.112,\ p<.001). This means that older adults with higher self-esteem were more likely to have increasingly higher life satisfaction when compared with those with lower self-esteem. The sociodemographic characteristics like gender, religious activity, and education level had significant effects on the slope of life satisfaction. Females had a higher slope of life satisfaction than males (b=.066,\ p<.001), and those who had religious activity also had a higher slope than those who did not (b=.037,\ p<.01). Meanwhile, the rate of life satisfaction appeared to be positively associated with higher levels of education (b=.029,\ p<.01). [/page/13/Text/4] In sum, in comparison with the oldest old, for the young-old, objective life conditions still had a significant impact on the slope of life satisfaction as subjective factors did.
